headline: Does seeing your ex hurt like a burn?
title: Social rejection shares somatosensory representations with physical pain
note: People who had recently been through a breakup looked at pictures of their ex and, in a separate task, received a painful heat stimulus. The authors interpreted overlap in some brain regions as evidence that rejection and physical pain share sensory representations. A later experiment found distinguishable multivoxel patterns for physical pain and social rejection despite overlap at the regional level. https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms6380

headline: Can the size of your amygdala give away your politics?
title: Political Orientations Are Correlated with Brain Structure in Young Adults
note: The researchers compared young adults’ self-reported politics with brain anatomy. They linked greater conservatism to a larger right amygdala and greater liberalism to more gray matter in the anterior cingulate cortex. Preregistered replication: in a sample of 928, the positive amygdala association was about one-third as large as in the original study. The anterior cingulate association was not consistently recovered. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2024.110532

headline: Nobody passes you the ball. Does your brain register pain?
title: Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion
note: Participants played a virtual ball-toss game. At first they got the ball, then the other players left them out. Researchers compared the two phases to ask whether social distress recruits regions associated with physical pain. A later study of rejection and physical pain found separate multivoxel patterns even in regions activated by both. https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms6380

headline: Does your brain choose before you know you have chosen?
title: Unconscious determinants of free decisions in the human brain
note: The authors decoded button choices before participants reported awareness of deciding. The task measured prediction of simple button choices relative to participants’ reported time of awareness. A separate line of work showed that the premovement readiness potential can arise in a stochastic accumulation model. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22869750/

headline: Do traders’ brains sound the alarm before a crash?

note: The authors measured neural responses to stand-up comedy videos and examined activity in reward-related regions.

headline: Does a luxury discount change the brain's response to a price tag?
title: The Effectiveness of Price Promotions in Purchasing Affordable Luxury Products: An Event-Related Potential Study
note: The researchers compared EEG responses to original and discounted luxury product prices with reported purchase intentions.

headline: Does buying an expensive gift for a lover produce a different brain response than buying one for a friend?
title: Deeper affection, more consumptions: consumer decision-making among people with different levels of intimacy-evidence from fNIRS
note: The study compared purchasing decisions and prefrontal activity for gifts to recipients with different relationship types.

headline: Does listening to music together synchronize the brains of friends?
title: Joint music listening enhances interpersonal affective and neural synchrony
note: Pairs of friends listened to selected music alone or together while researchers recorded fNIRS signals and pleasure ratings.

headline: Can your brain structure and activity predict the size of your social circle?
title: The social network-network: size is predicted by brain structure and function in the amygdala and paralimbic regions
note: The study compared several measures of social network size with brain measures.

headline: Can the brain tell you your place in a social hierarchy?
title: Know your place: neural processing of social hierarchy in humans
note: The study compared brain responses to ranks in a simulated hierarchy.

headline: Do men and women have different neural signatures of beauty?
title: Sex-related similarities and differences in the neural correlates of beauty
note: The paper compared neural responses to stimuli rated beautiful by men and women.

headline: Can brain responses to popular classmates predict later risk-taking and prosocial behavior?
title: Adolescents' neural sensitivity to high and low popularity: Longitudinal links to risk-taking and prosocial behavior
note: Examined neural responses to popular and unpopular classmates and changes in social behavior.

headline: Can brain scans reveal a lonely person's motivation to be included?
title: Let me in: The neural correlates of inclusion motivation in loneliness
note: Related loneliness and motivation for inclusion to brain responses during social interactions.

headline: Can brain scans predict how effective an anti-smoking message will be?
title: Neural Mechanisms of Emotion Regulation Moderate the Predictive Value of Affective and Value-Related Brain Responses to Persuasive Messages
note: Related responses to graphic anti-smoking messages to individual and public campaign outcomes.

headline: Can brain activity tell whether teenagers will talk about an anti-smoking ad?
title: Adolescents' Neural Response to Tobacco Prevention Messages and Sharing Engagement
note: Related fMRI responses to later discussion of the advertisements.

headline: Can brain synchronization explain why a student bonds with a teacher?
title: Affiliative bonding between teachers and students through interpersonal synchronisation in brain activity
note: The researchers measured teacher-student brain activity before and after instruction and examined changes in synchrony.

headline: Can brain scans show information flowing between classroom leaders and followers?
title: Bidirectional information flow in cooperative learning reflects emergent leadership
note: The authors used fNIRS and Granger causality to compare directional coupling among students during group learning.

headline: Do teachers and learners synchronize their brains by looking at each other?
title: Learning with others: teacher–learner brain synchrony depends on mutual gaze and joint attention
note: The study examined how gaze and shared attention relate to synchrony during teaching interactions.

headline: Does your brain distinguish actual curves from curves you think you see?
title: Neural dissociation between computational and perceived measures of curvature
note: The authors reanalyzed scans from a study of architectural preferences, comparing calculated and perceived curvature.

headline: Does learning to dance change the brain's appreciation of dancing?
title: Dance experience sculpts aesthetic perception and related brain circuits
venue: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
note: The authors compared dance training conditions and neural responses during aesthetic evaluation.
